newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Greenpeace urges action against EC on gene maize.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace urges action against EC on gene maize.

text.p: Greenpeace Austria urged European governments on Wednesday to take legal action against the European Commission after it approved the sale of gene-modified maize, which environmentalists fear may endanger human health.

"We are calling on countries to take the Commission to court because its ruling is in clear contradiction of the directive dealing with the release of genetically modified organisms to the environment," Matthias Schickhofer, spokesman for Greenpeace Austria told Reuters.
The approval of the grain by the EU Commission, with as yet unspecified labelling conditions, came after three teams of scientists said there was no reason to ban the maize.

The engineered maize will be imported from the United States where farmers have planted a type of corn developed by Swiss drugs firm Ciba Geigy AG, which is resistant to the herbicide glufosinate and the corn-borer pest and carries an antibiotic "marker gene".
Schickhofer called the decision "a total catastrophe".

"It is absolutely irresponsible as no security measures for labelling are included at all," he said. He demanded an immediate ban on the import of the corn, saying human health would be jeopoardised by the antibiotic-resistant grain.
Austria's health and environment ministries, which have been at odds recently over the issue of importing genetically modified soya, were united in slamming the EC decision.

"We are very unhappy indeed," said Michael Gerbavsits, spokesman for the health ministry. "We will investigate the arguments in depth, but the decision will come into effect fairly quickly," he added.

Environment minister Martin Bartenstein said the commission should have consulted EU environment ministers before reaching a decision and insisted Austria's initial doubts about opening the door to genetically altered maize still stood.
"From my point of view the issue of gene maize is much more critical than gene soya because of its resistance to antibiotics," he said in a statement.

Environmental groups and consumers across Europe have in recent weeks been up in arms over the import of genetically altered soyabeans from the United States, claiming the potential health risks of such products are as yet unknown.

Under the EU novel food law, food products for human consumption containing "live" genetically modified cells must be labelled. It also requires labelling for other bio-engineered food which differs from conventional foods "beyond accepted limits of natural variation".
The EU has not yet specified whether products derived from genetically altered maize would fall under this directive.

Austria, which sees itself as a trailblazer in environmental issues, has long been a vocal opponent of genetically modified foods. About half of all organic farms in the EU are located in Austria, and some 10 percent of the nation's farms are devoted to organic methods.
